I saw this movie on Amazon Instant Video. This movie is excellent and its story has a lot of ups and downs, the movie also has the famous western movie star Clint Eastwood. So I was mesmerized by the movie and recommend others to appreciate it.The movie has three leading roles which has different characters. The good person is called Blondie. The bad person is called Angel Eyes. The ugly person is called Tuco. The story happened during American Civil War, and developed gradually among the three western cowboys.Along with the story developing, a man tells the ugly man that there has a huge government wealth worth $200,000. The man tells the region of secret wealth, and the region named Sad Hill Cemetery has thousands of graves. However, the man does not tell the ugly man what the name of the grave which conceals the wealth, but tells the good man. Thus, the good man and the ugly decide to find the wealth jointly. Meanwhile, the bad man who disguises as a Union soldier also begins to find the huge wealth, and the three people meet in battle coincidentally. Then, they against each other by fist and gun fight intensely. Finally, after a lot of fights, the good man and the ugly man find the way to Sad Hill Cemetery.However, the way is blocked by the war between Union and Confederate, and the two forces fight constantly in order to occupy a bridge. Finally, the good man and the ugly man destroy the bridge by bombs. In the end, the bad man arrives in the region of secret wealth at the same time. The three cowboys decide to gun duel and the winner can get the wealth. Finally, the good man kills the bad man in the duel and releases the ugly man. The good man separate the wealth with the ugly man, and the good man leaves the ugly man in the desert. The final scene is that the good man rides his horse and disappears in the distance.The movie uses third person view to describe the fantastic story. The story depicts three different people deeply. They have different dispositions and distinguish each other brightly. The movie has a strong western atmosphere. For example, the whole story develops in the desert, and this is the typical character of the west of America. The three people have classic cowboy's appearance and trait. They have cowboy wear, especially the classic hat. They have a cool handgun and good gun skill. So they can hit a thin rope from a long distance. They judge other people with narrow eyes.This movie is different with former western movies. People do not divide to good or bad clearly. There is no a totally good person or a totally bad person. The good man also wants to gain the wealth and more money by fighting with others. The ugly man can be touched by some sorrowful things and help others by his own way. All people have two sides, good and bad. This idea in the movie causes big change in future western stories and movies. This movie also uses huge scenes to describe the most destructive of wars. Hundred thousand people die in the war and their bodies fall apart on the desert. This is a big satire of three people shuttle between two armies just in order to find the secret wealth. The movie also uses fierce gun fight to make the story ups and downs. For example, in the end, three people duel each other. They stare each other last 5 minutes and no one open the fire without careful thought. This scene makes audiences feel nervous and exciting.Personally, The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly is a very legendary movie and shakes me a lot. Thus, I saw the movie 3 times and think it is very wonderful. This movie not only is a lot of intense gun fight, but also reflects people's inner thoughts vividly. The three people have the same purpose but have different characters, so there are a lot of conflicts in the story. In the whole story, many scenes impress me a lot. For example, a command of Union is wounded in the war and will die soon. After the good man and the ugly man destroy the bridge between two armies, the command smiles and dies in happy. This sorrowful fragment reveals that people do not want to battle in war and they want to pursue peace. Another scene is that before the good man and the ugly man arrive in the destination, the good man meets a nearly dead soldier of Confederate. The good man puts his clothes on the soldier's body and gives his cigar to the soldier. The soldier smokes the final cigar and dies. This story tells us how the cruel is in the war.The movie also reflects the spirit of the Wild West. Like in the course book, the three cowboys are strong and do things without the law. They kill people cold and unconcerned. They are individual in most of time and there is no woman to accomplish them. They solve problems by dangerous fight or duel and do things what they want to. They are uncontrolled and use unscrupulous divisive tactics. They pursue the material wealth and have can-do spirit.I love this movie is also because of its wonderful music. In intense gun fight, the music is strong and curse. In sorrowful environment, the music is slow and emotionally. Especially before the end of movie, the ugly man run between thousands of graves to find the right name of the grave which conceals the wealth. The music describe the situation coordinately and becomes classic until today.You cannot miss this excellent movie, despite the language in the movie is Italian, but this does not block you to understand the story.

title_review: A Peerless Dovetailing - The Great Sergio Leone Directs The Great Clint Eastwood, Part 3
comment: Sooner or later, when you're discussing all-time great films, you MUST talk about the Man With No Name Trilogy!Eerily, each of the Man With No Name Trilogy films begins with several minutes of zero dialog, as if the silence were a direct parallel to the wasted landscapes.As a masterstroke, director Leone begins "The Good, The Bad, And Ugly" with the lone presence of the imposing Lee Van Kleef, or "Angel Eyes." And what are the viewers anticipating? The inevitable entrance of The Man With No Name! And sure enough, into the frame comes the great Clint Eastwood.Perhaps the greatest film ever made, "The Good, The Bad, And The Ugly" takes place in the heat of the American Civil War, & it pits a lone-wolf, a mercenary, & a Mexican super-outlaw against each other as they pursue $200,000 in buried, Confederate gold.In a particular scene of a Civil War battleground strewn pell-mell with corpses of young men, this viewer was particularly struck with the pathos of all those wasted lives!When The Man With No Name happens upon a very young soldier in the middle of dying, the movie almost rises to the level of great, elegiac poetry - it's an epiphany, really. It's the closest The Man With No Name will ever come to full-blown empathy & fellowship.The movie, of course, has to end with Angel Eyes, The Man With No Name, & the Mexican arch-villain ("Tuco") all in a stand-off in a Civil-War graveyard.Where the Hell is that treasure buried?This reviewer is not offering up any spoilers, so you'll have to watch the movie yourself.10 out of 10 stars! Maybe - just maybe - the greatest movie ever made!

title_review: Iconic Yet Imperfect: 'The Good, the Bad and the Ugly' Earns a Solid 7/10 for Its Western Legacy.
comment: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly straps you into a cinematic saddle for a thrilling journey through the rough and tumble of the Old West. Clint Eastwood's steely-eyed charisma and the iconic standoff scenes make it a must-see classic for any movie buff. Ennio Morricone's haunting score adds an extra layer of intensity, weaving seamlessly into the dusty landscapes and echoing the heart of this spaghetti western.However, saddled with a 7/10 rating, it's not a flawless ride. While the showdowns deliver the promised adrenaline, there are moments when the pacing slows to a meander. The film's commitment to the 'ugly' side of the West, though gritty and authentic, occasionally overstays its welcome. Yet, despite these bumps in the trail, the film remains a stalwart in the genre, a testament to its lasting impact on the cinematic landscape.

title_review: The worst in the series of excellent "Speghetti Westerns"
comment: This movie, unlike the two previous ("A Fist Full of Dollars" and "For a Few Dollars More"), is borish, long, contrived, and for once, the "Man without a Name" is anything but a good guy.  In this movie he's a liar, a thief and is more interested in money; compare this to the first movie where he is more of a quiet hero who ends up giving his money away to a girl, her husband and son and leaves town with nothing more than he came in with (although the town is cleaned up) and the second where, although less of a benefactor, he helps take down a vicious madman.  The story is a rampant anti-war film made in 1966, right when the war in Vietnam was really heating up.  The last two movies did not make themselves allegories (which rarely hold up as good classics over time) but rather well crafted short stories made into movies.Do yourself a favor and skip "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly".  It's one of those things where, until you see the movie, you won't realize how much worse the dialogue, pace and tempo is.

Beautifully shot and packed with a wickedly grim sense of humour this is one of the finest westerns this side of John Huston. Starring a stony faced don't-laugh-don't-blink Clint Eastwood and a crafty, weasely Eli Wallach it covers most of the genre's typical themes, albeit in a more gonzoid fashion, ranging from public hangings to duels and back.Sergio Leone goes to great lengths to create just the right atmosphere, filming even the smallest rolling tumbleweed if it improved on his vision. Consequently this an epic of epic length, which is bound to put some people off.However, the huge amounts of iconic moments, the sweeping Morricone soundtrack and the sheer wide-eyed sense of adventure it oozes turns it into a great slice of cinema.

Ennio Morricone's score is an integral part of the film's DNA. The hauntingly evocative theme music, particularly the iconic whistling, has become synonymous with the spaghetti western genre. Leone skillfully weaves elements of greed, loyalty, and betrayal into the plot, creating a tale that transcends the boundaries of a traditional western. The film's climax, set against the backdrop of a Civil War cemetery, is a cinematic triumph, a perfect blend of tension, action, and poetic justice."Il Buono, Il Brutto, Il Cattivo" is not just a western; it's a commentary on the nature of humanity, wrapped in the guise of a thrilling adventure. title_review: One of the Greatest Films Ever Made
comment: Ever since I first watched this film as a kid, I could feel the magic in it.It has everything-and more. It's one of those rare films you can watch again and again. A true epic.Its portrayal of the futility of war, of man's capacity for both humanity and betrayal, and of a crumbling Wild West stays with you long after the credits roll.Ennio Morricone's soundtrack is arguably one of the greatest ever committed to film. I defy anyone to listen to it and not be moved. It's so much more than just the iconic title track-it's a sweeping, emotional journey from start to finish.At its heart, the story follows three men in a relentless and almost mythical search for a fortune in buried gold. Their paths cross in ways that feel both destined and dangerous.Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef, and Eli Wallach are perfectly cast as the titular characters. Ask anyone to name a film starring any of them, and nine times out of ten, this is the one they'll mention-arguably their finest work.Sergio Leone directs with style, substance, and a touch of magic. Like all his films, this one is filled with bold visuals and unforgettable moments, but it stands apart for how it elevates the Western into something truly timeless.

title_review: Holy mother of god damn LIFE!!!!
The good, the bad and the ugly
comment: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly or the Good, the Better and the Best, as I prefer calling it, is a bizarrely sublime and a uniquely aesthetic masterpiece. The actors in title roles have given such extraordinarily superb performances, that it would be impertinent and disparaging to merely regard their swell work as acting. In fact their brilliant portrayals have immortalized Blondie, Sentenza/ Angel Eyes and the enigmatic Tuco. Lee Van Cleef is fiendishly unforgiving as the merciless Angel Eyes. Clint Eastwood is rugged yet suave, cocky yet adorable as laconic cigar-smoker Blondie, a role that laid the foundations of his illustrious career. But it is Eli Wallach, who steals the show with his captivating portrayal of Tuco, a portrayal that is as entrancing as it is enlightening. Wallach is amusing, capricious, nonchalant, uncanny and yet tenacious as Tuco, perturbed by his insecurities and dampened by his solitude. It is the tacit amicability between Blondie and Tuco and their mutual hostility towards the evil Angel Eyes owing to the vestiges of virtue present in them, redolent of their moribund morality, which gives the story, the impetus and the characters, a screen presence that is not only awe inspiring but also unparalleled.Sergio Leone's magnificent and ingenious direction in synergy with Ennio Morricone's surreal music, Tonino Delli Colli's breathtaking cinematography and Joe D'Augustine's punctilious editing makes the movie, a treat to watch and ineffably unforgettable. Initially aimed to be a tongue-in-cheek satire on run-of-the-mill westerns, The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, continues to stand the test of time in its endeavor to attain apotheosis (if it hasn't attained it yet). It will always be remembered as European cinema's greatest lagniappe, not only to the Western genre, but to the world of cinema.It's a must watch for any movie lover. 10/10.

The film masterfully blends action, suspense, and character development, with its three-hour runtime never feeling tedious. It's more than just a Western; it's a profound commentary on human nature, driven by survival, betrayal, and redemption. The iconic final showdown remains one of the most intense and stylistic moments in film history.Simply put, The Good, The Bad and The Ugly is a cinematic landmark, shaping the modern Western genre with its gritty realism, complex characters, and unforgettable score. The Good: Clint Eastwood stars as Blondie, the iconic "man with no name," embodying stoic, rugged morality. The film shines with its vast, sweeping cinematography, capturing the barren beauty of the American West. Ennio Morricone's legendary score is an essential component, creating a timeless, haunting atmosphere. Leone's direction brings intensity and artistry to every scene, particularly in the iconic Mexican standoff finale.The Bad: Angel Eyes, played by Lee Van Cleef, is a chilling, calculating villain, delivering a performance that perfectly contrasts Blondie's moral ambiguity. His portrayal is ruthless yet captivating, adding depth to the film's exploration of greed and survival.The Ugly: Eli Wallach's performance as Tuco adds a layer of complexity, comic relief, and unpredictability. His "ugly" nature is rooted in desperation, making him a memorable antihero who stands out in this trio of morally gray characters.

9,5/10. The final and best of Leone's "Dollar Trilogy". "The good the bad and the ugly" is not only a great war movie, not only a revolution in directing style, not only does it have an excellent script, not only is it massive in scope and spectacle for a western, not only did it set the standard for adventure films to come such as "Indiana Jones", not only does it have beautiful cinematography, but it just might have the greatest soundtrack of all-time.Everything is so masterfully crafted that it contains one of the most satisfying climaxes in cinema despite having little to no action at all. This should give you an Idea of just how impressive of a landmark this film is.Not everyone today knows this film, but everyone knows the climax and the music, since it has been parodied and payed homage to so many times in films such as Puss in Boots 2.My only gripe is how "the man with no name" escapes from Tuco through a plot convenience in one scene. Which is not only extremely unlikely considering how it was set up (without getting into spoilers) but mainly because it doesn't fit to have fate intervene, considering this is a film about the grayness of human morality (whether it's people, society or war) rather than a story about fate.But apart from that, objectively speaking, this is arguably the most consistent western ever made.And subjectively speaking, this film is tied with just a few other films to being my favorite film of all-time.

If there was just one film that was voted the best 3 hour runtime, that film might just be The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. The intriguing closeup shots of their faces, the striking soundtrack, the realistic sets and the great actors all contribute greatly to this film. Clint Eastwood makes you feel that he belonged in that time line and later directed another great western "Unforgiven." There is so much curiosity brung up in this film; we notice that Blonde is presumably "the Good", yet he lavishly joins the Ugly in a money scheme, and pays the price. We notice the "Bad" is really just doing his job and that the Ugly is the only one who has a discovered backstory in the film. The movie makes unexpected plot points to further show that there's so much more insight in the characters themselves and that they are not at all just plain characters that the previous two films used. That's what many westerns do; they attempt to immediately define characters with a specific trait and stand by it till the end. Sergio Leone finally does the right thing with Good, Bad and Ugly by taking full advantage of these traits, letting the viewers realize how important they really are.At its time, spaghetti westerns were treated like simple films and were not thought to be masterpieces. Roger Ebert commented on this, saying "I wrote a 4-star review for it, but gave it 3 stars, as it was a 'spaghetti western' and therefore could not be art. But art it is." As it gained a cult following, the film is often referred to as the greatest western ever made. How does Leone keep a viewer watching this movie? It's his fantastic directing and immersive story that makes any viewer love the fact they can watch this for so long.The direction fulfills the expectation of the audience using many techniques, all effective at most. Leone shows the film as if the characters know just as little as we do. They instead act rationally, if not understandably. None of the protagonists are exceptionally stupid; they seem to know they are in a film. When Blondie and Tuco are investigating the grave with the presumed money hidden, the Bad comes up suddenly. Blondie did the same before. But how couldn't they have noticed him if the distance was so far? The characters act the same way the audiences would, or better, as we want them to. When we are surprised, they are surprised. So the direction is heavily important in this instance. A scene where Blondie saves a threatened Tuco cuts to the protagonist handing him over to the government for bounty. A scene where Blondie is almost dead tired while walking through the desert. When the Bad discusses negotiations with the Good to work alongside each other. These are the moments where the characters surprise only us, as most films do. We witness breaks within characters, revealing their true selves. They know themselves, but we don't. That's the main thing that's hidden from us. I suppose since there was no need for it, Leone used it here as a plot device, yet another thing to keep the audience going. It is greatly effective.I realize how this film never wastes a single moment; every scene is moving on the movie quickly enough to keep us interested. Not a single dull moment exists in the movie. The actors were all obviously born to play their roles and they never break character ever. They're all so emotional in their roles, especially Elli Wallanch, who may just be the best character this film has got. The truth is, even the Bad shows great emotion.It's one of the best films you'll ever see.

title_review: The Good, the Bad, The ugly
comment: First released in Rome (12-66), home of its director (Leone), its USA premiere coming a year later (12.29.67) to complete the PEA-UA trifecta which began with A-Fistful-of-Dollars (Jan-67), then A-Few-Dollars-More (May), serving a full plate of the new spaghetti Western to audiences worldwide who feasted, turning the leads of its third and best entry into international celebrities.The year 1939 is tabbed best in film and it's hard to dispute with makes like Gone-With-the-Wind The-Wizard-of-Oz The-Women Goodbye-Mr-Chips Stagecoach and The-Hunchback-of-Notre-Dame. Then there's 1967, no runner-up as it produced more game-changers than any other: Guess-Whos-Coming-To-Dinner In-the-Heat-of-the-Night Bonnie-and-Clyde The-Graduate To-Sir-With-Love Cool-Hand-Luke and The-Good, a Western like no other, featuring an anti-hero that made the rest look like boy scouts. Filmed in Italy and Spain, terrain which compares to the southwest US, and scripted by a team of writers (Incrocci Leone Scarpelli Vincenzoni Donati Knox), Good had the biggest Produzioni budget and it shows.Set during the Western phase of the Civil War, it follows 2 non-combatants, Blondie the good (Clint) and Tuco the ugly (Eli) who partner in scam of criminal justice, then have a falling out, only to tenuously re-team in necessity when each is given partial clue to locating a buried Confederate gold shipment, swag also being sought by a well-informed, third gunslinger, the "tidy" bandito known as Angel Eyes (Lee). Shaky alliances form and fade, encountering family (Tuco's priestly brother) (Pistilli) and fighting along the way (a war weary Union Captain) (Giuffrè), culminating in a triangulated, graveyard showdown with only spirits of the dead in attendance to beckon new members. Most noteworthy for its performances in lead, signature English.

title_review: Leone, Morricone, Eastwood, Wallach, Van Cleef - the Western at its peak
comment: Watching a Sergio Leone Western is like sitting down for dinner Italian style the way Leone enjoyed it: You've got the whole family there, its slow but keeps coming and coming and the whole affair eventually lasts for hours - but you savor every minute of it.Part of the family are: Clint Eastwood ("the Good") of course in his third and final installment in a Leone movie, Lee Van Cleef ("the Bad") and Eli Wallach ("the Ugly"). Viewers familiar with the Dollar movies need no introduction to Eastwood's Blondie character, the gunslinger who spells cool, but his two adversaries/companions on the bounty hunt are on par in this one. Especially Eli Wallach steals the show with his twisted opportunistic, rough, down-to-earth, yet also outright funny performance, and Cleef's angel eyes never looked better and deadlier than in a Leone close-up underpinned by Ennio Morricone's extravagant, almost surreal soundtrack. The latter is a given considering Leone's previous collaborations with the master composer, but just as Leone's understanding on filming, Morricone's music reaches a new level in "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly". As for Leone: You've got it all here: The long shots over deserted lands, battlefields, hundreds upon hundreds of graves, counterbalanced by the extreme close-ups of characters digging deep into their minds and souls, plus there's the deliberate time the director takes to tell his story about greed, full of twists and turns, spiced up with irony. Unmissable.

title_review: Masterful tale about honor and morality!
comment:
This is it. Sergio Leones masterpiece. 
Why do I feel like writing the 841th review on this movie would change something? I don't know. 
Maybe it's just the feeling of having to publicly show my love for this film.
Saying that "The Good, The Bad and The Ugly" is a good film is a massive understatement. It is the best Western Movie ever made; But not just that. It is one of the best Movies ever made, period. The story is built and executed so perfectly that you don't even notice that the whole complex plot is just a simple storyline following three guys, each of them with different character traits than the other, chasing treasure. Yes, indeed, it is as easy as that. But how can a movie, with such a simple story, last nearly three hours? This is what makes "The Good, The Bad and The Ugly" so great. 179 minutes of screen time, but it never drags. There is no confidence in exactly knowing what is going to happen next. From the tough beginning, through the epic three way showdown. The time in between is paved with delightful bits of story telling, combined with classic, smooth and cool Western obligatory. The perfect mix of beautiful visuals and sadistic violence and brutality. I sadly didn't had the honor to see it in the theater/cinema but even on a TV screen the landscape is still one of the most beautiful sceneries in any motion picture. The violence is tough and of course there are lots of brutal death/fight scenes, but they are never distasteful. The humor is brilliant and the laughs keep coming although they are never fully essential. The movie score is up there with the best music scores in any other movie and it fits the movie greatly."The Man With No Name" is one of the best and iconic movie characters of all time. And Although I think there could be an argument made for Al Pacino's Michael Corleone in "The Godfather" as the best antihero in cinema history, "Blondie" takes the cake. 
"The Man With No Name, played brilliantly by Clint Eastwood is no hero. He has not the moral integrity of a hero, but he is a man of honor and respect. That makes him a character more relatable to, as we (as normal humans) probably also aren't heroes the way society in general wants us to be. 
It's especially "The Good, The Bad and The Ugly" that establishes the co-work of Sergio Leone and Clint Eastwood as one if the best, if not the best actor/director relationship along. That should not take away from the rest of the cast. Lee Van Cleef's "The Bad"/Sentenza is again, the perfect antagonist and Eli Wallach's "Tuco" just fits perfectly as the "third wheel". It's a tale about three men, that so often had the opportunity to kill each other, but never did that until the epic culmination.
Three guys just starring at each other and waiting for the other one's move; Priceless.If you read this review and now think 'Okay, this is a generic spaghetti western flick, with maybe some cool characters and visuals' you are so wrong. 
This would be like saying that "The Dark Knight" (2008) is a generic superhero movie, although it's NOT. Of course the movie's primary "use" is too be exciting, funny and gripping, but sometimes, there is just more to it than we think.
Sergio Leone brilliantly captures the cruel and pointless destructions of war. 
The movie shows that the war has no mercy, but in the end the war helps nobody. The melancholic atmosphere when "Blondie" and "Tuco" walk through the dead bodies, or the huge size of the cemetery just imply that. 
"The Good, The Bad and The Ugly" is a chess game, with little dialogue, but with so many iconic one liners that explain more than some overly long stretched dialogue. The most striking thing about the film is it's moral context. The way it presents each 3 characters but doesn't want to honestly separate all of them into "good" and "evil". It could be argued that "The Good" is "The Bad's" opponent. But who says that "The Good" is really 'good'? And what does "The Ugly" do, when there is already someone 'evil'? In fact, exactly this lawlessness and honesty describes and characterizes the film and perfectly develops all three characters. "There are two kinds of people in the world, my friend."
Summing up, "The Good, The Bad and The Ugly" is a perfectly paced, nearly flawless western classic, with unforgettable scenery, music score and characters. It is in my top 10 movies of all time and therefore rightfully deserves the perfect: 10/10
The sound track is the best part of this long, long movie. The use of the simple theme again and again works very well. However, in my opinion, it does not justify 2½ grueling hours!

The best western ever made period! In the last and the best installment of his so-called "Dollars" trilogy of Sergio Leone-directed "spaghetti westerns," Clint Eastwood reposed the role of a taciturn, enigmatic loner. Here he searches for a cache of stolen gold against rivals the Bad (Lee Van Cleef), a ruthless bounty hunter, and the Ugly (Eli Wallach), a Mexican bandit. Though dubbed "the Good," Eastwood's character is not much better than his opponents -- he is just smarter and shoots faster. The film's title reveals its ironic attitude toward the canonized heroes of the classical western. "The real West was the world of violence, fear, and brutal instincts," claimed Leone. "In pursuit of profit there is no such thing as good and evil, generosity or deviousness; everything depends on chance, and not the best wins but the luckiest." Immensely entertaining and beautifully shot in Techniscope by Tonino Delli Colli, the movie is a virtually definitive "spaghetti western," rivaled only by Leone's own Once Upon a Time in the West (1968).

title_review: Best Film ABOUT the Civil War Ever Made
comment: During his 25 years as a director, Sergio Leone directed only eleven films.  Remarkably, eight rate a 7.0 or better among IMDB members, and five are the on the IMDB Top 250 film all time best list!  GB&U is the highest rated of Leone films by IMDB subscribers.  GB&U is also the final segment of the most successful western trilogy ever made, the "man with no name" series; though GB&U is a prequel to the first film, A FISTFULL OF DOLLARS.  Narratively, I've always felt GB&U is the weakest of the series.  However, now that I have seen the DVD version with the excised scenes, I believe it is the strongest.  Two scenes in particular tie the film together.  The first, and most crucial, is a scene where Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef) visits a battle-damaged Confederate fort and is told the best place to find "Bill Carson" (if he is alive) is in the Union P.O.W. camp. So Angel Eyes appearance later in the film at the camp as the chief jailer makes sense.  The second excised scene shows Tuco (Eli Wallach) taking the horribly dehydrated Blondie (Clint Eastwood) to the nearest confederate camp, and finding out the mission where his brother lives is nearby.  Now, Tuco's assuming the identity of "Bill Carson" makes much more sense.I can still quibble with some other shortcomings of the film. Lee Van Cleef did such a terrific job as a the heroic Colonel Mortimer in the previous film in the trilogy, FOR A FEW DOLLARS MORE, it is almost impossible to accept him here as the cold- blooded killer Angel Eyes (Could the name be referring to the "Angel of Death?" The narrative never explains.)  Second, though Eastwood's hair is blonde in highlights, the name "Blondie" seems rather arbitrary and, again, jarring.  Still, these are minor quibbles about a film and a series that transformed westerns completely.  The influence of the "Man With No Name" series can be found in virtually every great western made since.Though the narrative is, on the surface, about three incredibly ruthless men pursuing $200,000 across a landscape of the Civil War, GB&U's underlying agenda is "anti-war", particularly the Vietnam War.  The film makes these points effectively without being offensively preachy.Critics of the time criticized the film for "putting a desert in the middle of the South."  What a crock!  Although not in thecenter of the War Between the States, quite a bit of action took place in New Mexico and Texas, and the film's writers even got the generals' names right!This is the handsomest of all of Leone's films, and that's saying a lot. The art direction and set decoration are particularly impressive, down to the mortars, gatling guns and naval-style artillary of the time.  Amazingly, CLEOPATRA, made four years before, cost almost 30 times as much! Never before or since have I seen so much of the budget up there on the screen.If you plan to see this film, make sure you watch it on a DVD with additional scenes.  You will need to turn on the English subtitles, since the cheap distributors didn't bother to hire "sound-alikes" to dub these "fill-in" scenes.  Hopefully, CRITERION will one day release a restored version of this films with the additional scenes inserted in the film where they belong.  After seeing the additional scenes, I raised my rating of the film from a "7" to a "9".  THAT'S how important they are.

title_review: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
comment: Set during the American civil war, 3 characters - 2 conmen played by Clint Eastwood and Eli Wallach and killer for hire Lee Van Cleef discover that a soldier called Bill Carson has buried $200,000 of gold in a cemetery somewhere. With each trying to get the treasure for themselves, they still keep crossing each other's paths, usually resulting in plenty of violence towards each otherGlorious and classic Leone western featuring 3 wonderful characters giving us great fun as they run into and try to outwit each other. Truth be told whilst each character is critical to the plot, this is Wallach's film. His fabulous 'bad guy' with a glint in his eye turn as Tuco gets the most screen time and is a particular pleasure to watch. There are though many great scenes in the film particularly the blowing up of the bridge and the cemetery which are pure cinema gold helped immeasurably by Morricone's legendary score and the horror of the war runs throughout adding a saddening seam to the story. A masterpiece.

title_review: slightly histrionic and very tedious - cleef is great though
comment: If it were not for Cleef's great pacing and character or Eastwood's humorous character development, this film would be considered a great failure (at least it would be in my humble opinion). the humor, the camera work, and the music, make this worth watching at least once.Unfortunately though, whatever pleasures one gains from the acting, is lost because Leone could not control himself when it came excessively long cuts. While he was clever and original in his cinematography and direction, his films would be much more tolerable had he spent some time studying under Hitchcock when it came to editing. Scenes that probably would have been 3 minutes during "A Fistful" became 6 minutes in "Few Dollars More" and 20 in "Good the Bad and the Ugly".Yes, the story is great, as it was in Few Dollars More, but the payoff in the cemetery at the end (while clever) is just not worth the price of excruciatingly long scenes of eyes and melodrama. Pale Rider and Josey Wales, even in their lamest moments, put this one to shame at its best.

In my opinion, this is the greatest western ever made. It's better than "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" and "High Noon". It really is that good. All three of the main performances, Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef and Eli Wallach are spot on. Being the last of the so-called "Dollars Trilogy", you get a sense that director Sergio Leone wanted to out do his first two westerns ("A Fistful of Dollars" and "For a Few Dollars More") by having everything in it, the American Civil War, a Treasure Hunt, and the best climatic shoot-out of all time. An interesting thing to note, is that it was the first Western Epic. Running out over three hours it was the longest Western of its time.If you haven't seen "Il Buono, Il Brutto, Il Cattivo" see it, if you have seen it, see it again now.

My parents first introduced me to The Good, the Bad and the Ugly a little over a decade ago. Since then, I've really loved it. And tonight, they took me to a theatrical showing of it at a local theater. And you better believe I still love it!!The movie is set in the American Southwest during the Civil War. A mysterious stranger, who goes by the alias "Blondie" (played by Clint Eastwood), and a Mexican bandit named Tuco Ramirez (Eli Wallach) form an uneasy alliance, in which Blondie hands Tuco in for the reward money, only to rescue him just as he is being hanged, and the two men split up the dough 50-50. But during one escapade, when Tuco greedily demands a larger cut of the bounty, Blondie replies by leaving him stranded in the desert. Enraged, Tuco hunts Blondie down and attempts to murder him in revenge. However, the two men abruptly rejoin forces to beat a sadistic criminal calling himself "Angel Eyes" (Lee Van Cleef), as well as the Union army, to find $20,000 that a soldier has buried in the desert.The acting in this movie is extremely choice. Clint Eastwood, who's amazingly still alive and well, is very cool and laid back as Blondie. Eli Wallach, may he rest in peace, is delightfully volatile as Tuco. And of course, Lee Van Cleef, may he also rest in peace, is a wonderfully chilling villain as Angel Eyes. The movie also features a really impressive supporting cast of people who collectively do great in their roles.In addition, the writing is top-notch. The movie is wonderfully violent and tense, especially in the gunfight scenes. One thing that really helps the dramatic moments is when there isn't dialogue, and the movie focuses exclusively on the characters' physical actions. But in addition, the movie manages to showcase a lot of clever humor when necessary, primarily from Tuco ("HEY, BLONDIE!!!! YOU KNOW WHAT YOU ARE?!"). Not much more that needs to be said here.And of course, there's the visuals. The movie boasts stunning cinematography, even for 1966, thanks to legendary Italian director of photography Tonino Delli Colli, may he rest in peace. Glorious wide shots give the audience a sense of the massive scale of the gorgeous American Southwest, while extreme close-up shots help build tension during confrontation sequences. It's a feast for the eyes, and always fits the tone the movie is going for.And lastly, the music! Italian composer Ennio Morricone, may he rest in peace, scored the movie wonderfully. His score is extremely fitting for a Western epic, especially his enduring, famous-for-the-ages main theme (Ooh-WOO-WOO-ooh. Wa-WA-wa.), which assumes specific guises for each of the three main characters throughout the movie. Of course, I had heard it in other movies prior to this movie (the first time I ever heard it being its downright blasphemous use in the movie Zoom), but no movie has ever used it as effectively as this movie does.Everything considered, The Good, the Bad and the Ugly is the gold standard for spaghetti Westerns! With Sergio Leone's stellar directing, wonderful performances from its three-man main cast and powerfully tense gunfights, this movie is a masterpiece that continues to hold up even by today's standards. Highly recommended!!!!!!

Sergio Leone's "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" is undeniably a very classic film. An iconic soundtrack. Very iconic scenes. The birth of the spaghetti western. The launch of Clint Eastwood's career. One of the many films that was partially responsible for the demise of the Hays Code in Hollywood and which gave rise to a new era of cinematic art through the 1970s to today. All of this is undeniable.And the film itself is quite excellent. The cinematography and editing and directing are all somewhat of a masterclass on film making here. This is one of the most beautiful films ever shot; a spaghetti epic that runs nearly three hours long.And that's part of my criticism with it. It feels a little bit longwinded. The pacing is slow. Many scenes that I feel are somewhat superfluous. The soundtrack is great but we here the same musical sequence like at least ten times in the movie, that crying harmonica. The dubbing is also pretty bad at times.I love it but I'll admit it's a little flawed and it's not something that I'd consider rewatching over and over again. It's a great film but at the same time it just doesn't really connect with me personally like I know it does for others.

title_review: Big surprise that got better and better
The Magnificent Seven of Spaghetti Westerns
comment: The Magnificent Seven: (The ones with Ennio music and (except for The Great Silence) Leone-directed or produced): A Fistful of Dollars 1964For A Few Dollars More 1965 The Good, The Bad and the Ugly 1966 The Great Silence 1968 (directed by Sergio Corbucci) Once Upon A Time in the West 1968 Duck, You Sucker! / aka A Fistful of Dymanite 1971 My Name Is Nobody 1973 (produced by Leone, he directed a few scenes) + 18 Honorable Mentions, making it a "Top 25": (a cut below Leone, but still good, most of which have at least one "Leone element" in them, mostly from the years 1965-1969, '66 and '68 being particularly banner years):A Bullett for the General 1968 (Gian Maria Volonte and Ennio music)Face to Face 1966 (Gian Maria Volonte and Ennio music) The Big Gundown 1966 (Lee Van Cleef and Ennio music) Death Rides A Horse 1968 (Lee Van Cleef and Ennio music) Day of Anger 1967 (Lee van Cleef) Sabata 1969 (Lee van Cleef) The Grand Duel 1972 (Lee van Cleef)The Mercenary 1968 (Ennio music) Run, Man, Run 1969 (Ennio music) A Pistol for Ringo 1965 (Ennio music)The Return of Ringo 1965 (Ennio music)Ace High 1968 (Eli Wallach) Under-appreciated (in the US, at least) Corbucci effortsNavajo Joe 1966 (Ennio music) Hellbenders 1967 (Ennio music) Companeros 1970 (Ennio music) Django 1966 Miscellaeneous (very good spaghettis with almost no "Leone elements") A Minute to Pray, A Second To Die 1968The Ruthless Four 1968 + 25 Other Spaghettis (not necessarily "good movies", but "of interest" due to "Leone elements", the participation of James Coburn, Eli Wallach, Charles Bronson, and Ennio Morricone being the most prominent) A Genius, Two Partners, and a Dupe 1975 (Ennio music, plus Leone may have directed a scene or two) The Guns of San Sebastian 1968 (Charles Bronson and Ennio music) Red Sun 1972 (Charles Bronson) Chino 1973 (Charles Bronson) Beyond the Law 1968 (Lee Van Cleef) The Return of Sabata 1971 (Lee Van Cleef) Long Live Your Death / aka Don't Turn the Other Cheek 1971 (Eli Wallach) The White, The Yellow, and the Black 1975 (Eli Wallach) A Reason to Live, A Reason To Die 1972 (James Coburn) Tepepa 1968 (Ennio music) Five Man Army 1968 (Ennio music) Sonny and Jed 1971 (Ennio music) What Am I Doing in the Middle of a Revolution? 1972 (Ennio music) Other vaguely interesting Spaghetti's mainly due to the cast involved: Adios, Sabata 1970 *Yul Brynner A Bullet for Sandoval 1969 *Ernest Borgnine A Man Called Sledge 1970 *James Garner Deaf Smith and Johnny Ears 1973 *Anthony Quinn The films of the "other Sergio", Sergio Corbucci (plus The White, The Yellow, and the Black, Sonny and Jed, and What Am I Doing in the Middle of a Revolution? mentioned above, are of interest for mainly historical reasons.) Massacre at Grande Canyon 1963 Minnesota Clay 1964 Ringo and His Golden Piston / aka Johnny Oro 1965 The Specialist 1968 The "Comedy Spaghettis" with the Terence Hill/Bud Spencer, known as the "Trinity" films (Whether you find these Hill/Spencer westerns funny or not is a matter of taste. The Italians love them, I personally prefer the first three more serious Westerns they made in the 60's to the Trinity films. I have already mentioned Ace High which also stars Eli Wallach, above. Actually, it was part of a non-comedy trilogy with the Hill/Spencer team. Boot Hill and God Forgives, I Don't are the other two.) God Forgives, I Don't 1968 Boot Hill 1969 They Call Me Trinity 1971 Trinity is Still My Name 1971 ------------------------------------------ *Well that's it for the "top 50". Actually, I'm not so sure about 26-50, but 1-25 are must see and rock-solid. If you can't get enough of this type of movie, rather than wasting your time with the mostly substandard 400 to 500 hundred remaining Eurowesterns (the vast majority of which stink to high heaven), I would recommend trying the Clint Eastwood films Hang 'Em High (1968), Two Mules for Sister Sara (1970), Joe Kidd (1972), High Plains Drifter (1973), Outlaw Jose Wales (1976), Pale Rider (1985) and Unforgiven (1992). Obviously, they aren't spaghetti westerns, but the Leone kinship is obvious. Think of them as the Leone/Eastwood films they never got around to making together.Also, the films of Sam Peckinpah, especially, The Wild Bunch (1969), The Ballad of Cable Hogue (1970) and Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid (1972), which were also key films in the "deconstruction" of the Western. Oh, McCabe and Mrs. Miller (1971) by Robert Altman is another key film.P.S. By all means, avoid Spanish "Paella" Westerns, which are even worse than the very worst Italian made ones. Especially A Town Called Hell (1971) by Eugenio Martin, it is absolutely lousy despite the stellar cast.P.P.S. Contrary to what some people may try to tell you, there are no Late Spaghetti Classics (after 1973). No, Keoma, Four of the Apocalypse and China 9, Liberty 37 are not lost classics, they are pretentious, preposterous failures, deservedly (and mercifully) forgotten. The two post '73 spaghettis I did mention were only due to the involvement of Leone and Corbucci, I wasn't endorsing those films necessarily.

title_review: Great Score - shame about the film.
comment: 3 men out west seek hidden loot in the civil war.The Good the Bad and the Ugly starts brilliantly, with each of the three in question shown in their own opening scenario. Eastwood is quickly established as the 'Good', Van Cleef the 'Bad' and Eli Wallach as the 'ugly'. Though generally there's no difference in their characters, as they all steal, kill and betray. Blondie (Eastwood) and the ugly repeatedly steal from the law by collecting ransom demands for the latter, not stopping at one to forgo the increasing value on his head. Van Cleef murders anyone for money. There a rather spirited bunch. From their on the experience becomes tedious and very slow. There are some great set-pieces including a battle on a bridge involving hundreds of extras, and the standoff at the end is excellently done, with extreme close-ups that heighten the tension. Once again the Italian scenery is efficiently, if excessively used. It's just a shame that it's alloyed by Wallach's hamming and a ten minute scene of Eastwood crossing the desert - sound exciting ?. The film is badly dubbed but even this doesn't mar the enjoyment as much as Ugly's cringe worthy sentimental scene with his brother, superfluous ? -not entirely. It does lead to some 'Good-Ugly' relationship humour which is where most of the film gets it's laughs. To be fair, none of the humour seems out of place with all the explosions and blood as the film doesn't take itself entirely seriously (Sergio Leone seems to have been satisfied with the over-the-top performances by virtually every character except Eastwood and Van Cleef). But this doesn't matter - because the score is one of the best for any western ever.

title_review: Too Bad Eli Wallach Ruined the Movie!
comment: Clint was on a tear in the 60s with his spaghetti westerns. He proved a washed-up American TV idol could reinvent himself successfully and end up rich enough to make splatter movies for decades before doing a few artsy films for fun. I'm unsure of his politics, but the man has to have bad dreams always. I detested them when they came out; now, I find them amusingly quaint considering how vulgarly violent the newer films have gotten. Unfortunately, these films brought about the disintegration of morals/manners in the world, an antihero crazy society and the notion that only very wealthy people can make a film anymore. They are essentially a very bad thing for humanity, but there's no turning back now.Eli, Eli, what made you think you could pull off a Mexican accent/persona? You are a joke. The NYC grit is still there but mixed with spicese, it becomes a very bad scene. Your tristate accent cannot be squelched. You sound like you're about to hail a cab at any second. And you're just not mean enough, dear. You're basically a teddy bear and it shows. Did you owe Eastwood a favor or did he offer you a bundle? It's very sad because your performance drags down what might have been a more interesting film.

I was battling weather to give this movie a 4 Â½ or 5, so I gave it the benefit of the doubt. Once you get that high in my books, itâ??s pretty much the same. The movie was amazing and was one of the best western movies I have seen. It runs three hours and although it did feel long, it wasnâ??t a bad thing. I kept on wanting to follow the characterâ??s journey to the end and find out what was going to happen, regardless of how long it took. The acting was great and the soundtrack was phenomenal. It added to the films mood immensely.This film obviously has inspired many modern filmmakers today (Rodriguez, Tarantino, among others) and I had to keep on reminding myself that this film was made in 1966. I either thought it was made with todayâ??s film techniques or some scenes were actually shot during the civil war time period. It really took me back and followed it up with a great story.The actors gave dialog in their native tongues and as a result there is a poor voice over synchronization throughout the movie. I found this slightly distracting at times, but it did not deter me from enjoying the film and Sergio Leoneâ??s great filmmaking brilliance shone through. The sweeping panoramic shots were incredible and appealing throughout the film as well.Although I loved the characters Blondie - The Good, played by Clint Eastwood and Angel Eyes - The Bad, played by Lee Van Cleef; Tuco - The Ugly, played by Eli Wallach had an absolutely great performance and pushed the film to a greater level.

A truly magnificent 3 hour long tale of three bandits, on the trail of half a million dollars in stolen confederate gold. Clint Eastwood is Blondie, a mercenary gunman who partners up with the Mexican bandit Tucco (Eli Wallach) to play a con on several different western towns. Tucco plays the part of captured bandit, Blondie the part of bounty hunter who has captured the wanted criminal. Subsequently he collects the reward, and Tucco is to be hung. But being a con, naturally Blondie just shoots Tuccon down off the hangman's rope, and into the sunset they ride to their next con job. Into the fray rides Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef playing the role to menacing perfection), a ruthless killer on the trail of the stolen gold after two of the thieves turn on each other, both hiring Angel Eyes to murder the other. He may be a ruthless killer, but he does have a perverted sense of honor, and thus fulfills both contracts, but not before one of the men tells him the story of the stolen gold, and whom he should seek out to get it, another thief in on the heist, who has now joined up with the Confederate army. As the broad backdrop of the Civil War rages on, we are given a microcosm of the conflict with not two, but three competing sides. What's interesting here is the dichotomy of the characters being almost mirror images of one another. Each a skilled gunman, and proficient killer. However, what separates the three is the degree of morality each has; Blondie killing only when necessary, when he's confronted with no other choice. Tucco kills for convenience, his life of crime has made him many enemies, so he's often faced with the end result, those out for revenge. But Tucco has a softer side, and we see several revelations about his upbringing that place him in a somewhat more heroic light than he first comes across as. Finally, there's Angel Eyes, a demonic killer with no empathy, sympathy or moral direction. He's out to get everything in life for himself, and will sell out anyone that tries to stop him. He delights in torture, but seldom sullies his own hands. He prefers to let others do the dirty work, and enjoys the spoils. I really think he's a representation of the Devil. Someone that enjoys manipulating, killing and causing chaos. A being totally involved with the pleasures of life regardless of the cost to others. The film's climax with a Mexican standoff is priceless, and the entire film is a enjoyable, riveting experience that should be on the beginners list for Western film viewing. Interestingly enough, it is so deep and nuanced, it can easily go onto an Experts list for WEstern viewing as well.

The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly, stars Clint Eastwood as Blondie, Eli Wallach as Tuco, and Lee Van Cleef as Angel Eyes.This movie is a masterpiece, and represents the qualities that good movies should exhibit. It's written with an interesting story, great character development, great character interaction, and great production values.This movie is about 3 gunslingers who at times work together, or against each other in search of a bountiful treasure hidden in a secluded cemetery. At different points of the movie, Blondie and Tuco work together, then betray each other, then come to work together again. At other points of the movie, Angel Eyes works together with Blondie, leaving Tuco as the out man.The story begins before Tuco and Blondie meet up. After meeting, they then work together to collect bounties on Tuco who is worth $1000s. The team can split the bounties as they move territory to territory scamming the law. With each new town, Blondie collects the bounty, then saves Tuco from actually being put to death, then they divide up the bounty.Problems begin as greed sets in. With in a short time, Blondie abandons Tuco after rescuing him, even after Tuco warned him to never betray him and leave him alive. Eventually, the roles are reversed, and it is Tuco who abuses Blondie and nearly causes his death.But this is where the story takes a major twist, as a run away wagon with a nearly dead passenger reveals secrets of a treasure, but each Tuco and the half dead Blondie only learn a vital part of the secret from. So now Tuco must save Blondie to get to the treasure.The story continues from there, and we get to learn quite a bit about the characters. Especially Tuco, in my opinion Leone purposely allowed us to see that indeed there were no defined roles as who was "the good", "the bad", and "the ugly". Greed is very powerful, especially when life is such a struggle to begin with.The final showdown is unbelievable. It is epic, and is absolutely worth anything to see. It's the pinnacle of movie making, the showdown, the movie, the characters, the drama building. Truly a masterpiece.This movie is great, it's a cinematic masterpiece. As of this writing, it's #16 in the top 250 movies on IMDb, and deserves to be. Any western fan must see this movie, no excuses. Any fan of movies in general must see this movie, no excuses.Thank you Sergio for making this movie.10/10
"If you gonna shoot, shoot, don't talk". An epic western, it has it all; shootouts, gold coins, and a dysfunctional dynamic duo.

A good Clint Eastwood, a bad Lee Van Cleef and an ugly Eli Wallach carry Sergio Leones masterpiece to greatness.This is a true classic with timeless perfomances and of the most epic moments in cinema history. It's of course the final duel between the trio. Not to mention The Good, The Bad And The Ugly has one of the greatest soundtracks ever, composed by the great Ennio Morricone, who in my opinion composed some of the greatest movies themes ever: "The ecstasy of gold", Main theme and "The Trio" theme.The Good, The Bad and The Ugly is one of the most important movies ever made and all the westerns you watch are partly inspired by this film (even Quentin Tarantino says this is one of the most inspiring movies, it's also one of his favourites).The Good, The Bad And The Ugly is the best western ever made and one of the greatest movies ever.10/10.

title_review: A very good western but overlong
comment: This takes place during the American Civil War (but was shot in Spain). Three men (Clint Eastwood, Eli Wallach and Lee Van Cleef) form an uneasy alliance. They don't trust each other and all hate each other but they all want $200,000 hidden away in a cemetery. The first hour is introducing the three characters--the remaining two hours deal with their journey.This has been called an epic and operatic western. I agree! It's beautifully directed by Sergio Leone. He knew how to frame shots and use the wide screen perfectly. Most of the film is told by images not dialogue. Heck there's no dialogue for the first 10 minutes! There's plenty of shoot outs and action. The acting is OK. Eastwood was never a great actor but he's OK here. Wallach gets annoying but that's his character. Van Cleef is just so-so but has little screen time.There's one big problem here--the length. There is no reason for this to go on for three hours. Scenes ramble on inconclusively quite a bit. There's also a long battle scene and talk with a drunken captain that add nothing to the main storyline. The battle scene is impressively done but it's not needed. Still it's an epic and should be seen at least once. Recommended.

In this world, there's two kinds of people, my friend - those who like spaghetti westerns and those who don't.  Personally, I think this is one of the greatest films ever made.  Nothing can match Sergio Leone's masterful direction, the twangy score by Ennio Morricone, or the ever-cool presence of Clint Eastwood.  It's near enough perfect. There are also memorable performances from Eli Wallach and Lee Van Cleef, who as always has an air of menace about him.  The film is also packed full of memorable moments - such as the climactic final showdown - and there is plenty of wry humour to keep you amused as well as amazed. Idiots?  It's for you!

title_review: Can justifiably be called the best Western ever.
comment: Sergio Leone's epic tale of three men all on a different point of the morality scale is a thoroughly entertaining film that is certainly one of the best in its genre, if not one of the best films overall.Clint Eastwood completes his "trilogy" of roles with Leone as Blondie, the quiet drifter who has few friends and plenty of bullets. In every scene, Eastwood's quiet yet brutally tough nature shows that he is one of the brightest stars of the last fifty years, and even though he has gone on to become a better director than actor, he still deserves to be considered a great actor.All the acting is terrific, with Lee Van Cleef perfectly intimidating as the hit man Angel Eyes, and Eli Wallach stealing the show as the comically-violent bandit Tuco. They carry the story along and Leone paces it so well that even though it is quite long, it is well worth it to see the final sequence of the showdown between all three characters.And of course, we cannot forget to honor the man who made this series possible. All throughout, Sergio Leone shows his enormous talent as a director and filmmaker. He certainly changed the genre forever with this film, and that is just one reason of why this may be the best Western ever made.

I've read ALL of the posts. Took a while. Some eloquently summed up exactly what I thought of this truly great film. Others seemed to dwell upon minor points that intrigued the writers.All are worthy of their place.No summing up of the film.No point in that.All I can try to do is place my feelings upon a page...The musical score - NEVER has there been a soundtrack which has set my emotions aflame such as this one. From the 3 individual themes which seem to sum up all there is about the characters in question to the lament over the death of a soldier to the greedy excitement of the discovery of the cemetary & finally the brooding menace of the final showdown. The master @ work. The direction - close-ups, pan-backs, no talking for first 10 mins, the vistas, the scope, the grandeur...no, I could go on & on... The cast - all were perfectly cast - in fact I read in the biog by Patrick Agan that this was written to be the vehicle for Clint to true stardom. It is a pity that Eli did not have that boost as much. And as for Lee Van Cleef - never have I seen death so close up!For me there is absolutely NOTHING wrong with this film save perhaps that it ends (in true & fitting style - off into the sunset - or at least the distance).

title_review: One of the best? No. Potentially one of the best? Absolutely.

comment: Come on you guys, ok, everyone was a-ok, Clint, Eli, Lee, they knew their words and acted their characters, camera angles, set dressing wonderous, but friggin story to convolutive, too out there, fighting the war or fighting each other, to many slow angles. I had only seen bits and pieces, but I watched the whole thing last night and found it real, but too long, and so many unanswered story points. title_review: ENTER: THE MAN WITH NO NAME.
comment: One of the longest westerns ever filmed, but you never get tired of the adventure, if not the insanity. Tale of human nature at its worst, with a wry smile, under even worse conditions -- the scorching desert.Applause tenfold to director and writer Sergio Leone, who began his career as an assistant to legends like Mervyn LeRoy, Robert Wise, William Wyler, Raoul Walsh and Fred Zinnemann, working in Italy on various film projects.In rides the Man With No Name, superbly played by Clint Eastwood, who must deal with two bandidos, played to the hilt by Eli Wallach and Lee Van Cleef. The rest is cinematic history. The "speghetti western" defined, film-making at its creative best. Superb characters, script and casting, right down to the bit players. Meticulously planned. Hits the bullseye.An interesting footnote; Leone may have been inspired by Hitchcock's films, incorporating a few select examples here, definitely a dark comedy slant to this classic. Best line goes to Eli Wallach, delivered while he's in a bathtub(!) no less.... "If you're going to shoot, shoot! Don't talk!"The cemetery scene where the Confederate gold is buried is now legend. The third and final installment of the "Dollars" film series, preceded by A FISTFUL OF DOLLARS and FOR A FEW DOLLARS MORE.Memorable music score by Ennio Morricone that lives to this day. One of the most prolific film composers. Leone followed with ONCE UPON A TIME IN THE WEST.Always on dvd and remastered blu ray.MGM dvd includes deleted scenes from the original Italian release. 2 hrs 41 min. 2005. Thanks to TCM for running this adventure of all adventures since the beginning.

This movie is the best of the best, the greatest of the great, it has everyhting you could dream of, and it's actually one of the most entertaining pcitures in the market. It's one of those movies you want to see a remake of, but not changing anything.
The film shows you it isn't needed an intricate plot or a side romance to be the best movie ever. It has so many memorable quotes and moments (the best being the final shootout).
It was snubbed at the Oscars in everything:
Clint Eastwood for best actor (Clint Eastwood really gives a thrilling performance)Eli Wallach and Lee Van Cleef for best supporting actor (they both are at his best here, and there could have been easily been a tie between this two contenders). EVEN ADOLF GIUFFRÉ GIVES A FINE PERFORMANCE IN THE 10 MINUTES HE APPEARS ON THE FILM.Ennio Morricone for best original score (perfect music, perfectly used for every moment, reaching its climax in the shootout).Sergio Leone for best director (the way this movie is directed, mmm I would have paid to be on set with this beast of a director)Tonino Delli Colli for best cinematography (every single scene is a visual masterpiece, 2nd of the decade only to Lawrence of Arabia)Carlo Simi for best costume design (the confederate costumes, the cowboys costumes, the way the bandits dress, it's all so stunning)Sergio Leone, Agenori Incrocci, Furio Scarpelli and Luciano Vincenzoni for best original screenplay.Anyway, I think I have made my opinion pretty clear, considering it among the best 5 movies of all time.
Hope is useful!!!

My heart always skips a beat whenever I think about this movie.Oh man! While I live in a reality far far away from the canvas of this movie, it will remain my favourite, and of many generations to come.

title_review: Want to watch a western? Watch any of Leone's films. Want to watch the western? Watch this one.
comment: The epic conclusion to the trilogy of the nameless men brings together everything that worked in the previous films and avoids all the mistakes. As the result of this evolution, I will discuss that progression by comparing it to its predecessors.In the first film, there was little mystery, the plot went straight into action, and the main character was so cold that little of him could be seen. In this one, however, we have three distinct characters, each defined by a single dominant trait, as reflected in the film's title. The Ugly does things in ugly ways. He is petty, sly, treacherous, and not particularly smart, but full of street smarts. The Bad is a man who takes pleasure in cruelty, is intelligent, and knows when to strike. And finally, the Good is a man with principles, but who does not let them stand in the way of what must be done. The story of these three not only intertwines, it completes itself. Everything that happens has a reason, and eventually all the pieces fall into place.The second film carries greater narrative weight, though not fully developed. In this one, secondary characters have relevance, there are memorable moments, and a sense of mystery that gives the film narrative flow and a strong sense of time.Finally, the use of setting and the epic tone. With each film in the trilogy, the landscape grows. In the first, the setting is well constructed. In the second, it expands, and narrative elements interact with it, becoming symbolic at times. In this final film, the symbolism is striking, critical tones are subtly embedded, and the script creates moments that weave together all the elements mentioned before.Absolutely brilliant.

title_review: Another drop dead classic by Leone.
comment: I rated the first two episodes of the 'Dollars' trilogy 10 out of 10! The third for me was just a shade under, due to a larger epic feel and the fact that apart from the most memorable title track, the musical score was not consistently as great. When i say great, I mean to the genius level of the former 'Dollar' Westerns. Good western. The western vocabulary was mature and popular well before movies, and with the detective story drove the first revolution in modern mass publishing. Its simple abstractions were converted to film (then radio and TeeVee) without change: the boy scout cowboy in the usually white hat, often singing. (In fact the modern pop country music borrows from this simple vocabulary and reference to the 'genuine.') But all that, including the country music bit is pretty flat, stupid and dull.Italian cinema is based on a similar set of national icons, specifically religious icons. It is a more visual, visceral painterly vocabulary. Equally simple in stereotypes, but instead there are religiously based connections that give the impression of depth. Symbology is expected, even demanded. To this add postwar notions of irony which permeated European popular art. So the good guy was still good, but in a twisted way -- the twists shifting according to the chaos he encountered.In the US, John Ford was creating soft lush panoramas that would subliminally inspire a generation of environmentally aware viewers, but something more important came rushing in from Japan: Kurosawa. His films are abstract, directly evolved from Japanese watercolor narratives. These are also lush and beautiful, but not soft -- instead dusty, gritty, sometimes cruel. This world is not placid, merely a machine to test color and honor.7/10.

title_review: The Good, The Bad And The Ugly: One of the best
comment: Once every few years, a movie pops up that thousands or maybe even millions consider to be one of the best films ever made. The Good, The Bad And The Ugly is definitely one of those few. Blondie (Clint Eastwood), Tuco (Eli Wallach) and Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef) are three men who are in search of gold coins that are buried in a cemetery. However, each man only knows a certain amount of information as to where the gold is and are therefore dependent on each other.The Good, The Bad And The Ugly is an incredibly suspenseful movie and will have you on the edge of your seat throughout. The action scenes are top-notch and really kick in the tension. The famous showdown at the cemetery seriously had me guessing as to what the hell was going to happen to the point of being wide-eyed and I'm sure that it's the most suspenseful scene in cinema history.Although Clint Eastwood gives an excellent performance as Blondie, it's Eli Wallach who shines as Tuco. The audience has a strange, ever-changing relationship with his character. At some points (mainly early on) we hate his guts and at other points we love him and can't get enough of him. He actually had me laughing quite a few times such as when he takes a desperate but brilliant measure to break free from his handcuffs. I won't ruin it for you, but it involves a train.Even if you haven't seen the movie, you WILL recognise its theme tune. Ennio Morricone's music is one of the best things about The Good, The Bad And The Ugly and its theme tune is certainly among the greatest of all time.The thing that amazed me about the film is that it keeps you entertained and interested throughout its three hour length. Films this long tend to get boring after a while and you eventually just lose interest, but TGTBATU will make you ask for more. Anyway, more to love.I haven't seen the movie's predecessors A Fistful Of Dollars and For A Few Dollars More. I've heard good things about them, but I have to say that it would take A LOT for them to be better than this cinematic masterpiece.The Good, The Bad And The Ugly is one of the best movies ever made and is also one of my favourite films. I give it 10/10.

title_review: Authentic in its Ugliness, Intense in its Badness and Operatic in its Goodness ...
comment: INTRODUCTION :A nasty face full of scars and sunburns suddenly fills the screen, covering the extended vision of the Sierra landscape : a curious opening, creating two incongruous feelings of authentic yet comical ugliness. This sums up the very essence of the 'Western Spaghetti', a pivotal sub-genre that traced the singular evolution, hence the survival, of the Western genre in two polar opposite directions : the "anticonformity" and the "overconformity" or let's just simplify and say "demystification" and "amplification".DEMYSTIFACTION: Akira Kurosawa's innovative "Yojinbo" ended the classic 'good vs. bad' antagonism, which directly inspired Sergio Leone. Like "A Fistful of Dollars", the realism of "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" lies within the lack of morality of the three main characters, each of them has malicious motives. Leone's intuition over using Kurosawa's characterizations proved to be useful for the Western genre that was begging for a metamorphosis. John Ford's era was over, and with all due respect to John Wayne, everyone knew how the West was Won, and were tired of the pompous idealism displayed, despite the breath-taking imagery of Monument Valley. Even the mythic Civil War, the powerful symbol of the fraternal fight that ultimately consolidated the American spirit, is treated like a vulgar subplot, which somewhat betrays the foreign aspect of the film, and in the same way, sweeps off all the dust of semi-propaganda stuff disguised in entertainment. The myth was agonizing, and the 'Western Spaghetti' genre proceeded to a sort of creative destruction.Take the three main characters, the irony in the title, is that all their 'nicknames' are interchangeable, there is something ugly in the bad, and vice versa, and the good isn't 'boy-scout' good. Listen to the opening credits, flute for Blondie, Clint Eastwood as the Good, ocarina for Sentenza, Lee Van Cleef as the Bad and human voices for Eli Wallach as Tuco, the Ugly. Different instruments were used for each but they all play the same iconic melody, inspired from the howling of a coyote. Symbolically, each character is different, but the deadly greed inhabiting their hearts is the same, it's "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" rather than "The Good vs. the Bad vs. the Ugly". Their relationships are all tactical, cynical and hypocritical, with friendships based on a mutual need to reach a hidden gold. The Good and the Bad need each other, because they know half the secret about the gold's location, and Sentenza, need them alive to find it. They're all tied to each other until the strongest and cleverest wins; this was the humanistic reality during the dark ages of the last century.AMPLIFICATION: I guess the fact that I watched it for the first time when I was 10, built my personal affection to the film, because at that age, my expectations were not tarnished by the cynicism of the classic know-it-all film buff. For me, the three characters were not similar; the Good was the hero, the Bad, the villain, and the Ugly, the comic relief. They happen to be the only recognizable actors' faces in the film, but it hardly matters because we don't need them overshadowed by other supporting performances. Eli Wallach, in a career-defining role, is the fastest talking and provides the best moments of the film as the indisputable scene stealer. His humor also relies on the exciting duo he formed with Blondie whose cool sense of humor, and cynical detachment proved at many occasions to be the yin to Tuco's yang. And Lee Van Cleef is the senseless, cold-blooded killer who makes the Ugly look Good. He represents the dark side of the film, a man who always finishes his job, and from the first scene involving him, I took him as the bad guy of the story. The characterization is why I loved the film both as a kid and as a movie buff.The line between amplification and parody is very thin, but there's a difference. When parody takes all the conventions into derision, amplification insists on them, providing the typical Leonesque shots. Time is dilated, locations are magnified, like belonging to a unique dimension, and the whole film oscillates between extreme close-ups and extended shots from very far away. All the effects are amplified with cinematic hyperbolas exceeding the limit of believability. In his 'Great Movies' review, Ebert stated that Leone invented a rule which consisted on the characters' point of view limited by the screen. I never understood until I re-watched the film and got it, and I respect Leone even more for having pushed the limits of creativity to this point since most of the greatest effects from the film depend on that rule, and are transcended by the iconic score of the musical genius, Ennio Morricone. "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" has all the tragic, comic, epic and musical elements that makes it a kind of operatic masterpiece.CONCLUSION :Film-making is far from being an exact science, and you can make a masterpiece out of the least complex plot elements, the lowest budget, and the cleverest directorial tricks. Not to diminish the quality of Leone's "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" but the point is that the movie works as if it was self-aware of its own restrictions and transcended it with a magic that another director, wouldn't have judged necessary. Some apparent weaknesses are sometimes the necessary drivers to push the creation to the limit of genius while confidence can work as a tricky obstacle, maybe that explains why "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" is the highest ranked Western on IMDb Top 250 and undoubtedly the most iconic.So, to conclude, I would simply say that there's two kinds of people in this world, those who love the film, and those who don't get it ...

title_review: My favourite movie of all the stuff I have seen in my lifetime.
comment: Hello friends. I am a long time IMDb user and in October 2020 it will have been for 15 years. After watching the Mulan (2020) remake I sat here and I wrote my review in mild disgust. I then proceeded to evacuate my bowels for 45 minutes in a strange but calming grip of horror that maybe the mastery and art of cinema is completely dead.However, what comes to mind is the Ojibwe saying from 'The Sopranos', which is: "Sometimes I go about in pity for myself, and all the while, a great wind carries me across the sky." I also realised that I haven't made many written reviews, even though I have watched and rated as of right now 2,781 titles.In any case, I had decided to celebrate 15 years of me using IMDb by reviewing all the titles that I have rated a 10 out of 10 perfect score. A change of pace. A palette cleansing. There aren't many titles, mind, as I have noted here only 8 that fit the bill... out of 2,781. There are of course a whole bunch of good titles that I have given a 9/10, and I will probably list those later on.So here we go, the 8 titles that I gave 10/10 are as follows: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966), The Sopranos (1999-2007), Jaws (1975), The Shield (2002-2008), Seven Samurai (1954), The Shining (1980), Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964), and finally The Passion of the Christ (2004).The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly. This is an adventure, with crazy characters, good music, a backdrop of civil war, and most of all a treasure hunt.I love the character development in this title, each of the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly have their own motivations, and mix in a whole load of grey area in between. I can't really explain it, but these three characters might be some of my favourites. I want to feel sorry for Tuco, but he's a wild animal. I want to root for the man with no name, but he is so ambiguous. I feel as if Segio Leone knew what he was doing in this regard, a commentary on the psychology of man and in particular the time period of the frontier west.The attention to detail is ahead of it's time I feel, the longshots, and the rapid editing in the showdowns. This has been copied and copied time and again, but Lerone did it first I feel. His camerawork and positioning are top notch.I love the backdrop, and I love the composition of music, scenery and atmosphere. This is masterful and well balanced. I'm almost certain he has encoded the 7 sins in this movie as well. Story wise the three main characters intertwine several times and end up on the same goal of finding the gold coins. I can't understand how well this plays out and the slow burn to the final showdown is just pure genius. I love this movie, and will continue to watch it until I die.In any case, this is a perfect 10 out 10 film, certainly the best 'Western' ever created.
